readerTitle: Why a rainy week can make a clothing brand order three times too many jackets
caseNote: 가상 사례 (의류 브랜드의 수요계획팀, 철물 체인의 물류센터) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 공급망 결정은 주문서가 아니라 계산대 판매를 보고 내려야 하며, 상품마다 버퍼를 둘 곳과 빠르게 대응할 곳을 나눠야 한다.
misconception: 매장 주문이 늘면 수요가 늘어난 것이니 공장 주문도 그만큼 늘리면 된다. 재고 전략은 모든 상품에 하나로 정하면 된다.

sources.text: 공급망 관리의 표준 개념 (채찍 효과, 적시 생산 vs 예비 재고)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 3번 카드의 증폭 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 고객 +10% → 매장 주문 +30% → 지역 창고 주문 +60%로, 단계마다 주문이 커지는 흐름만 보여 줍니다. 실제 연구 수치처럼 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.
리드타임(원거리 공장 12주, 근거리 공방 3주, 선풍기 공급사 2주)은 모두 가정입니다. 실제 업계 평균으로 제시하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: One rainy week, three times the orders.
body: Mira leads the planning team at a mid-size outdoor clothing brand. After a wet week, a yellow rain jacket starts selling well in the north.
By Friday, the warehouse is asking for far more jackets than the stores ever sold. Somewhere between the shop floor and her desk, a small rise became a big one.

image.label: A yellow rain jacket on a rack, with order slips growing larger behind it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 매장 옷걸이에 노란 우비 한 벌. 뒤쪽으로 주문서 종이가 단계마다 점점 커지며 이어짐 (작은 영수증 → 큰 주문서 → 거대한 주문서). 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Orders for the jacket are up 60%.
body: The regional warehouse wants 60% more yellow jackets next month. The factory needs 12 weeks to make them, and the rainy season may be over by then.
What should Mira's team do?

options.text: Order 60% more now, before the factory fills up
options.feedback: You'd secure stock fast, but you'd be reacting to orders, not sales. That is the **bullwhip effect**: small swings grow at every step, and the jackets may land after the rain stops.

options.text: Pull register sales from the stores first, then size the order
options.feedback: This costs a day or two but shows real demand. Looking past orders to actual sales is how you stop the **bullwhip effect** from reaching the factory.

options.text: Split the difference and order 30% more
options.feedback: Less risk than A, but still a guess built on inflated orders. The number is only safer if it comes from sales data.

cards.title: Each step added its own cushion.
body: Shoppers bought only **10% more**. Each link ordered a little extra to be safe, and the extras stacked up.

breakdown.label: Shoppers
breakdown.detail: Jackets actually sold at the registers

breakdown.label: Stores
breakdown.detail: Managers ordered extra so they wouldn't run out

breakdown.label: Warehouse
breakdown.detail: Saw store orders jump and added its own buffer

cards.title: The bullwhip effect, up close
body: Nobody lied. Each person made a sensible choice with the information in front of them: the orders from the step below.
That is the **bullwhip effect**. A flick at the handle becomes a crack at the tip. The fix is to share the same signal with everyone, which here means register sales.
Mira's team now gets weekly sell-through, the share of stock that actually sold, from every store.

image.label: A whip whose wave grows from store to warehouse to factory
image.brief: 채찍 그림 인포그래픽. 손잡이 쪽에 "Shoppers"(작은 물결), 가운데 "Stores", "Warehouse", 끝에 "Factory"(큰 물결). 물결이 점점 커지는 모습.

cards.title: Planning next season: two very different products.
body: A plain black T-shirt sells steadily all year. A bold printed dress could be a hit or a flop.
The usual overseas factory is cheap but takes 12 weeks. A nearby workshop takes 3 weeks but charges more per piece. How should the team stock them?

options.text: Small, frequent orders for both, to keep stock lean
options.feedback: Lean works for the dress. For the T-shirt, a 12-week factory and steady demand mean frequent small orders risk empty shelves on your most reliable seller.

options.text: Keep a buffer of T-shirts from the far factory; make a small first batch of dresses and reorder nearby if they sell
options.feedback: This mixes **just in case** for the predictable item with near **just in time** for the risky one. You pay more per dress, but only for dresses people want.

options.text: Order big on both so nothing ever runs out
options.feedback: **Just in case** protects sales, but on an uncertain dress it can mean racks of markdowns and cash tied up in stock.

cards.title: Just in time and just in case can live in one brand.
body: The choice isn't one policy for the whole company. It's a choice per product.
Steady, predictable items with long lead times earn a buffer. Uncertain items with a fast option earn small bets and quick reorders.
Mira's team now sorts every product into one of two groups before placing a single order.
cards.softwareNote: An online store or app business makes the same split with computing capacity: reserve the steady baseline cheaply in advance, and buy extra on demand for spikes. And one big customer's one-off job can look like growth, which is the bullwhip effect in a dashboard.

cards.title: Both fixes have a price.
body: Sharing sales data needs systems and trust. Store managers may worry that honest numbers will cut their allocations.
The nearby workshop costs more per piece, so it only pays when it prevents bigger losses from markdowns.
And a buffer only helps if it sits in the right place. A thousand T-shirts in the wrong warehouse still leave a store's shelf empty.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware chain before a heat wave.
body: You run the distribution center for 25 hardware stores. A heat wave is forecast in five days, and store orders for fans have tripled. The supplier needs two weeks to deliver more.
What do you do?

options.text: Ship every store what it asked for and order triple from the supplier
options.feedback: Stores get fans fast, but tripled orders are inflated by fear. That's the **bullwhip effect**, and the reorder lands after the heat has passed.

options.text: Send each store a share based on its own recent fan sales, and hold the rest centrally to move where fans actually sell
options.feedback: Sales data tames the **bullwhip effect**, and a central **just-in-case** buffer goes where demand shows up. You'll make some extra trips, but fewer fans sit unsold.

options.text: Ship normal amounts until sales prove the spike is real
options.feedback: This avoids overreacting but ignores a real, short window. By the time the proof arrives, the heat wave may be over.

cards.title: Order from sales, and buffer by product.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **The bullwhip effect:** react to what customers buy, not to what the step below orders. **Just in time vs just in case:** hold buffers for steady items, place small fast bets on uncertain ones.
**Try it today:** pick one product. Compare last month's orders from your customers or stores with what actually sold to end buyers. How big is the gap?
